content_metadata.description: An informative video featuring Park Ranger Ashlyn as she guides viewers through a hike in Zion National Park during winter, emphasizing safety tips, preparedness, and the beauty of the natural landscape.

qAndA.answer: Traction devices are crucial for navigating the icy sections of the trail, especially the final ascent to Angels Landing, which is always shaded and prone to ice.
qAndA.question: What is the most important piece of gear for hiking Angels Landing in winter?

qAndA.answer: Temperatures can change quickly in Zion, and wind chill can make it feel much colder than the actual temperature. Extra layers provide warmth and help prevent hypothermia.
qAndA.question: Why should hikers bring extra layers even on sunny days?

qAndA.answer: The sign marks the point beyond which hikers require a permit to continue on the Angels Landing trail. It indicates a more challenging and potentially dangerous section of the hike.
qAndA.question: What is the significance of the sign Park Ranger Ashlyn points out at 1:22?

qAndA.answer: Park Ranger Ashlyn repeatedly emphasizes that safety is each individual's own responsibility. The scene of the hiker slipping highlights the consequences of inadequate preparation, and the inspiring music and visuals in the final scene encourage viewers to make smart choices for their own well-being.
qAndA.question: How does the video create a sense of personal responsibility?

qAndA.answer: The video blends informative and cautionary elements with a sense of excitement and wonder. While highlighting the potential dangers of winter hiking, it also showcases the beauty and allure of exploring Zion National Park in the snow, encouraging viewers to approach the experience with both caution and enthusiasm.

Plan to prepare for whatever might come your way. This means bringing a backpack with all sorts of gear with you, whether that’s a first aid kit, extra water, food, snacks, extra layers and make sure to check the weather before you come as well. Even if there hasn’t been precipitation in the past few days prior to your hike there may still be ice and snow present. We have had ice on the Wiggles and on Angels Landing the entire season even though we’ve only had precipitation a few times. So make sure you’re bringing traction devices to be able to you safely get up that You want to make sure that the toe is right over and centered. Pull it right on up on and over and adjust as needed you want to make sure that there’s no jingling, which means that the spikes are too loose, and you want to make sure that they’re nice and tight. We often see visitors trying to make it up Walter’s Wiggles without traction. That often does end up in a precarious situation. A lot of folks end up slipping and sliding on their way down, and it can present a dangerous situation especially for those hikers who are hiking up as people are trying to come down. Permit required past this point. You can come as far as Scout Lookout but once you are touching chain that is where the permit starts, for the next half mile. On this  section it’s going to have some steep drop offs and ridges that you’re going to be traversing, there is also going to be a lot of ice patchy ice. So, there may not be ice in every section but there’s definitely going to be enough that you’re going to want traction on this section for sure. The final assent to Angels Landing never gets sun so there are some spots that will have some very thick ice that you want to be cautious of as well. I say if you want to summit you need traction with you. Your safety is your responsibility so whatever you feel like you need to stay safe is really important. Whether that’s actually extra layers whether that’s a pair of gloves to keep your hands warm as a gripping the chains on the way up, it’s really your call on making sure that you stay safe here in our national parks.

youtube_description:
Hiking in Zion this winter? Planning a trip for spring break? Zion is experiencing snowpack levels nearly 200% higher than average according to the Utah Department of Natural Resources. Expect trails in the park to have snow or ice, even if the forecast is sunny. 

Park Ranger Ashlyn takes us up the West Rim Trail to Angels Landing and to show just how icy and snowy trails can be even after days of sun. 

The best thing to do before your hike is plan like a ranger: bring traction devices, layers, plenty of food, and water.
